content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›Endpoint Types Overview
Core Concept

Global Accelerator Endpoint Types

Connecting Global Accelerator to your AWS resources

Application Load Balancers (ALB)

Ideal for HTTP/S traffic, providing Layer 7 features like path-based routing and SSL termination. Combines global routing with advanced application-level features.

Network Load Balancers (NLB)

Best for high-performance TCP/UDP traffic, operating at Layer 4 with ultra-low latency and static IP support. Suitable for gaming, IoT, and VoIP applications.

EC2 Instances & Elastic IPs

Directly use individual EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses as endpoints. Less common for scalable applications, typically for specific or legacy use cases.

Why Endpoint Choice Matters

  • Protocol Compatibility: Match endpoint type to your application's protocol (HTTP/S for ALB, TCP/UDP for NLB).
  • Performance Needs: NLBs offer extreme performance for latency-sensitive applications.
  • Scalability & Features: ALBs and NLBs provide built-in scalability, health checks, and advanced routing.
  • Cost Efficiency: Choose the most appropriate endpoint to optimize resource utilization and cost.
Key Takeaway

Selecting the correct endpoint type is fundamental for optimizing Global Accelerator's performance, availability, and cost-effectiveness for your specific application needs.

screens.title: Global Accelerator with Application Load Balancers (ALB)
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating Global Accelerator with Application Load Balancers, or ALBs, is a highly effective pattern for delivering web applications globally with enhanced performance and resilience. Global Accelerator directs HTTP and HTTPS traffic to the nearest healthy ALB, which then distributes these requests to your target EC2 instances or containers. This combination is powerful because the ALB provides crucial Layer 7 features, such as path-based routing, host-based routing, and SSL termination, allowing for sophisticated application-level traffic management. Meanwhile, Global Accelerator handles the global routing optimization and performs health checks at the network layer, ensuring users are always directed to the best available endpoint. For example, imagine you have an e-commerce website with ALBs deployed in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Global Accelerator will automatically route users from North America to the us-east-1 ALB and users from Europe to the eu-west-1 ALB. If the us-east-1 ALB or its targets become unhealthy, Global Accelerator seamlessly fails over traffic to the eu-west-1 ALB, providing continuous availability without relying on slow DNS changes. This setup combines the best of both worlds: Global Accelerator's global performance and static IPs with ALB's advanced request routing and application-level health checks.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›ALB Integration
Integration Pattern

Global Accelerator with Application Load Balancers (ALB)

Optimizing web application delivery globally

Key Benefits

  • Global Performance: Routes users to the nearest healthy ALB over the AWS global network.
  • Layer 7 Features: Leverages ALB's path-based routing, host-based routing, and SSL termination.
  • Automatic Failover: Seamlessly redirects traffic to healthy ALBs in other regions upon failure.
  • Static Anycast IPs: Provides a consistent entry point for your application.

Example Scenario: Global Web App

An e-commerce platform uses ALBs in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Global Accelerator routes North American users to us-east-1 and European users to eu-west-1. If us-east-1 fails, traffic automatically shifts to eu-west-1, ensuring continuous service.

How it Works

Global Accelerator directs HTTP/S traffic to the ALB. The ALB then distributes requests to target EC2 instances. Global Accelerator performs network-level health checks, while the ALB handles application-level health checks and routing.

UserGlobal AcceleratorALBEC2 Targets
Key Takeaway

Combining Global Accelerator with ALBs provides a robust solution for global web applications, offering advanced routing, SSL termination, and automatic regional failover.

screens.title: Global Accelerator with Network Load Balancers (NLB)
screens.narratorSegment: For applications demanding extreme performance, ultra-low latency, and high throughput, especially those relying on non-HTTP/S protocols like TCP, UDP, or TLS passthrough, integrating Global Accelerator with Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, is the optimal choice. NLBs operate at Layer 4, the transport layer, and are engineered to handle millions of requests per second with consistent, low latency. They also provide static IP addresses for your load balancer, which can be crucial for certain network configurations. When Global Accelerator directs traffic to an NLB, it leverages the NLB's ability to forward traffic directly to target EC2 instances or containers with minimal processing overhead. This makes the combination particularly beneficial for use cases such as real-time gaming, IoT device communication, or Voice over IP, where every millisecond counts and consistent network performance is paramount. For example, a global multiplayer game could use Global Accelerator to route players to the nearest NLB, which then efficiently distributes game traffic to backend game servers. This ensures players experience the lowest possible latency, regardless of their geographic location, and provides a highly available and scalable backend for the game. The key benefit here is combining Global Accelerator's global network optimization with NLB's raw Layer 4 performance.

Module 11›Chapter 11.5›NLB Integration
Integration Pattern

Global Accelerator with Network Load Balancers (NLB)

Achieving extreme performance for TCP/UDP applications

NLB Advantages for GA

  • Layer 4 Operation: Handles TCP, UDP, and TLS passthrough traffic efficiently.
  • Ultra-Low Latency: Designed for millions of requests per second with minimal latency.
  • Static IP Support: Provides a stable IP address for the load balancer.
  • High Throughput: Ideal for applications requiring massive data transfer.

Use Case: Real-time Gaming

A global multiplayer game requires consistent, low-latency connections. Global Accelerator routes players to the nearest NLB, which then efficiently distributes TCP/UDP game traffic to backend game servers, ensuring optimal player experience.

How it Delivers Performance

Global Accelerator directs traffic to the NLB, which operates at the transport layer (Layer 4). This allows for direct forwarding to target instances with minimal processing, making it highly efficient for latency-sensitive and high-throughput applications.

UserGlobal AcceleratorNLBEC2 Targets
Key Takeaway

For latency-sensitive TCP/UDP applications, Global Accelerator with NLBs provides unparalleled performance, throughput, and consistent low latency.

screens.title: Direct EC2 Instances and Elastic IPs as Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: While Application and Network Load Balancers are the preferred endpoints for most scalable and highly available applications, Global Accelerator also offers the flexibility to use individual EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses directly as endpoints. This approach can be suitable for very specific scenarios, such as a single dedicated server that doesn't require the full features of a load balancer, or for legacy applications that are not designed to sit behind a load balancer. For example, you might have a specialized licensing server or a bastion host that needs a static global entry point without the overhead of an ALB or NLB. However, it's crucial to understand that using direct EC2 instances or Elastic IPs as endpoints comes with limitations. You lose the built-in scalability, advanced health check mechanisms, and fault tolerance that ALBs and NLBs inherently provide. If the single EC2 instance fails, Global Accelerator will reroute traffic, but you'd need to manually manage the replacement or have other mechanisms in place. Therefore, while this option exists, it's generally recommended to leverage the robust capabilities of ALBs or NLBs for any application requiring high availability, scalability, and comprehensive health monitoring. Always evaluate your application's specific needs before opting for direct instance endpoints.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›Direct Endpoints
Endpoint Options

Direct EC2 Instances and Elastic IPs as Endpoints

Understanding specific use cases and best practices

When to Use Direct Endpoints

  • Single Dedicated Server: For applications not requiring load balancing.
  • Legacy Applications: Systems not designed for ALB/NLB integration.
  • Specific Services: Bastion hosts, licensing servers, or niche services needing a static global IP.
  • Simplified Setup: For minimal overhead in non-critical environments.

Example: Global Bastion Host

A company needs a single, globally accessible bastion host for secure access to private networks. By using an EC2 instance with an Elastic IP as a Global Accelerator endpoint, they get a static Anycast IP for consistent, low-latency access from anywhere in the world.

Limitations & Best Practices

  • Limited Scalability: Direct instances don't offer inherent auto-scaling.
  • Manual Fault Tolerance: Requires external mechanisms for instance replacement.
  • Basic Health Checks: Global Accelerator performs direct health checks, but lacks advanced application-level monitoring.
  • Recommendation: For highly available and scalable applications, prefer ALBs or NLBs.
Key Takeaway

While direct EC2/EIP endpoints offer flexibility for niche cases, ALBs and NLBs are generally superior for scalable, fault-tolerant, and highly available global applications.

screens.title: Global Accelerator Health Checks
screens.narratorSegment: A critical component of Global Accelerator's ability to deliver highly available applications is its robust health check mechanism. Global Accelerator continuously monitors the health and responsiveness of all configured endpoints. This proactive monitoring is essential for ensuring that user traffic is always directed to a healthy and operational application instance. For endpoints like Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers, Global Accelerator intelligently leverages their existing health check mechanisms. This means if an ALB determines that its backend EC2 instances are unhealthy, Global Accelerator will recognize this status. For direct EC2 instances, you configure specific health checks within Global Accelerator itself, defining the protocol, port, and path to monitor. The real power of these health checks comes into play during a failure. If an endpoint becomes unhealthy, Global Accelerator automatically and almost instantaneously stops routing traffic to it. Instead, it redirects traffic to another healthy endpoint, either within the same endpoint group or to a different endpoint group in another AWS Region. This automatic failover is significantly faster and more reliable than traditional DNS-based failover, which can suffer from DNS propagation delays due to TTLs. For example, if a database issue causes your application in us-east-1 to become unresponsive, Global Accelerator detects this and reroutes users to your healthy application in eu-west-1 within seconds, minimizing downtime and impact on your users.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›Health Checks
Availability Feature

Global Accelerator Health Checks

Ensuring continuous application availability

How Health Checks Work

  • Continuous Monitoring: Global Accelerator constantly checks endpoint health.
  • Leverages ELB Checks: For ALBs/NLBs, it uses their integrated health check mechanisms.
  • Direct EC2 Checks: For EC2 instances, configure protocol, port, and path directly in GA.
  • Automatic Failover: Unhealthy endpoints are automatically removed from traffic routing.

Example: Regional Application Failure

An application in us-east-1 becomes unresponsive due to a backend issue. Global Accelerator detects this via health checks and instantly reroutes all user traffic to a healthy replica in eu-west-1, minimizing service interruption.

Benefits of GA Health Checks

  • Faster Failover: Network-level routing avoids DNS propagation delays.
  • Enhanced Reliability: Ensures traffic only goes to truly healthy endpoints.
  • Simplified DR: Automates a critical part of disaster recovery.
  • Improved User Experience: Reduces downtime and latency during regional outages.
Key Takeaway

Global Accelerator's health checks are vital for high availability, enabling rapid, automatic failover to healthy endpoints, significantly improving application resilience.

screens.title: Managing Traffic with Traffic Dials
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond automatic health-based failover, Global Accelerator provides another powerful feature for traffic management: traffic dials. A traffic dial is associated with each endpoint group, which typically corresponds to an AWS Region. This dial allows you to specify the percentage of traffic that Global Accelerator sends to that particular region. By default, a traffic dial is set to 100%, meaning the region is fully active and eligible to receive traffic. However, you can adjust this percentage to achieve various traffic management strategies. For instance, setting a region's traffic dial to 0% effectively takes it out of service, preventing any new traffic from being routed there, even if its endpoints are healthy. This is incredibly useful for maintenance, testing, or disaster recovery scenarios where you want to explicitly control traffic flow. You can also use traffic dials for controlled rollouts, gradually increasing the percentage of traffic to a new region or a new version of your application. Imagine you're deploying a new feature in ap-southeast-2. You could start by setting its traffic dial to 10%, monitoring performance, and then slowly increasing it to 50% or 100% as confidence grows. This granular control allows for sophisticated and safe deployment practices, minimizing risk during changes.

keyIdea.title: Traffic Dials: Regional Control
keyIdea.text: Traffic dials allow you to specify the percentage of traffic routed to each regional endpoint group, enabling controlled rollouts, maintenance, and active/passive or active/active strategies.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›Traffic Dials
Traffic Management

Managing Traffic with Traffic Dials

Granular control over regional traffic distribution

What are Traffic Dials?

  • Regional Control: Each endpoint group has a dial to set traffic percentage.
  • Default 100%: Region is fully active and receives traffic.
  • Set to 0%: Effectively takes a region out of service for new traffic.
  • Granular Adjustment: Allows for precise control over traffic distribution.

Example: Controlled Rollout

A new application version is deployed in eu-central-1. Initially, its traffic dial is set to 10%. After successful monitoring, it's gradually increased to 50%, then 100%, ensuring a safe and controlled rollout process.

Use Cases for Traffic Dials

  • Maintenance: Temporarily divert traffic from a region for updates.
  • Testing: Route a small percentage of users to a new environment.
  • Disaster Recovery: Manually shift traffic to a standby region.
  • Capacity Management: Adjust traffic based on regional load or capacity.
Key Takeaway

Traffic dials provide powerful, granular control over how Global Accelerator distributes traffic across your regional endpoint groups, enabling flexible operational strategies.

screens.title: Active/Passive Failover Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most common and effective architectural patterns enabled by Global Accelerator and traffic dials is the active/passive failover strategy. In this setup, you designate one AWS Region as your primary, or active, region, which handles all normal operational traffic. A secondary, or passive, region is configured as a standby, ready to take over if the primary region experiences a complete outage or becomes unhealthy. To implement this, you would set the traffic dial for your primary region's endpoint group to 100%, ensuring all traffic flows there under normal circumstances. For your secondary, passive region, you set its traffic dial to 0%. This means Global Accelerator will not route any traffic to the secondary region unless a failover event occurs. The magic happens when Global Accelerator's health checks detect that all endpoints in the primary region have become unhealthy. In such a scenario, Global Accelerator automatically and instantly shifts all traffic to the healthy secondary region, even though its traffic dial was set to 0%. This provides a much faster and more reliable disaster recovery mechanism than traditional DNS-based failover, which can be hampered by DNS propagation delays. For example, if your primary application in us-east-1 goes offline, Global Accelerator ensures users are quickly redirected to your standby application in eu-west-1, minimizing business disruption.

keyIdea.text: Active/passive architecture uses Global Accelerator to route all traffic to a primary region (100% dial), with a secondary region (0% dial) acting as a standby for automatic failover upon primary failure.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›Active/Passive
Architecture Pattern

Active/Passive Failover Architecture

Designing for robust disaster recovery with Global Accelerator

Active/Passive Configuration

  • Primary Region: Traffic dial set to 100% (active).
  • Secondary Region: Traffic dial set to 0% (passive/standby).
  • Health Checks: Global Accelerator continuously monitors both regions.
  • Automatic Failover: If primary fails, traffic automatically shifts to secondary.

Example: DR for a Critical Service

A financial service runs in us-east-1 (primary) with a replica in us-west-2 (passive). If us-east-1 experiences a major outage, Global Accelerator detects the failure and reroutes all client connections to us-west-2, ensuring business continuity.

Benefits for Disaster Recovery

  • Rapid Recovery: Significantly faster failover than DNS-based methods.
  • Consistent Entry Point: Static Anycast IPs remain the same during failover.
  • Reduced RTO: Minimizes Recovery Time Objective by automating traffic redirection.
  • Simplified Operations: Global Accelerator handles the failover logic.
Key Takeaway

Active/passive failover with Global Accelerator provides a robust and rapid disaster recovery strategy, ensuring minimal downtime for critical applications.

screens.title: Active/Active Distribution Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: In contrast to active/passive, an active/active distribution architecture leverages Global Accelerator to simultaneously serve traffic from multiple AWS Regions. This pattern is designed for maximum availability, geographic redundancy, and efficient load distribution across your global infrastructure. To implement this, you configure endpoint groups in two or more regions, and set their traffic dials to percentages that reflect their desired load distribution or capacity. For instance, you might set traffic dials to 50% for two regions, or proportionally based on the expected user base or available resources in each region. Global Accelerator then intelligently routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint across all active regions. This means a user in Europe would be routed to the European region, while a user in Asia would be routed to the Asian region, assuming both are healthy and have traffic dials set appropriately. The key benefit here is that all regions are actively serving traffic, providing continuous service even if one region experiences a partial or complete outage. If one region becomes unhealthy, Global Accelerator automatically directs all traffic to the remaining healthy regions. This not only enhances fault tolerance but also improves user experience by routing them to the closest available endpoint, reducing latency. For example, a global SaaS platform could run active instances in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-2, with Global Accelerator distributing traffic among them based on user proximity and health, ensuring optimal performance and high availability worldwide.

Architecture Pattern

Active/Active Distribution Architecture

Achieving global redundancy and load distribution

Active/Active Configuration

  • Multiple Active Regions: Endpoint groups in 2+ regions, all with traffic dials > 0%.
  • Proportional Dials: Set percentages based on capacity or desired load distribution (e.g., 50/50).
  • Nearest Healthy Endpoint: Global Accelerator routes users to the closest healthy active endpoint.
  • Continuous Service: All regions serve traffic simultaneously.

Example: Global SaaS Platform

A SaaS application runs in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-2, all with 100% traffic dials. Global Accelerator routes users to their nearest region, providing low latency and ensuring continuous operation even if one region experiences issues.

Benefits of Active/Active

  • Maximum Availability: No single point of failure across regions.
  • Optimal Performance: Users routed to the geographically closest endpoint.
  • Load Distribution: Spreads traffic across multiple regions, preventing overload.
  • Enhanced Fault Tolerance: Automatic rerouting to remaining healthy regions during outages.
Key Takeaway

Active/active architecture with Global Accelerator delivers superior availability, performance, and load distribution for truly global applications by utilizing multiple regions concurrently.

screens.title: Global Accelerator for Disaster Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Disaster recovery, or DR, is a critical concern for any global application, and Global Accelerator significantly enhances DR strategies by providing a faster and more reliable failover mechanism compared to traditional DNS-based approaches. The primary challenge with DNS-based failover is propagation delay. When you update DNS records to point to a new region during a disaster, the changes can take minutes or even hours to propagate across the internet due to Time-To-Live, or TTL, settings and caching by DNS resolvers. This delay directly translates to downtime for your users. Global Accelerator, however, operates at the network layer, not the DNS layer. It provides static Anycast IP addresses that remain constant, regardless of which AWS Region is actively serving traffic. When a primary region fails, Global Accelerator's health checks detect the issue and instantly reroute traffic to a healthy endpoint in a secondary region. This rerouting happens within seconds, bypassing DNS propagation delays entirely. For example, if your primary data center in us-east-1 becomes unavailable, Global Accelerator ensures that your users' traffic is almost immediately directed to your standby application in eu-west-1, minimizing the impact of the disaster. This capability drastically reduces your Recovery Time Objective, or RTO, making Global Accelerator an invaluable tool for building resilient, business-critical applications.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.5›Disaster Recovery
Strategic Advantage

Global Accelerator for Disaster Recovery

Faster, more reliable failover than traditional DNS

Traditional DNS Failover Challenges

  • Propagation Delays: DNS changes can take minutes to hours due to TTLs and caching.
  • Inconsistent Experience: Users may experience varied downtime depending on their DNS resolver.
  • Manual Intervention: Often requires manual updates during a crisis.
  • Higher RTO: Longer recovery times due to inherent DNS limitations.

Example: Regional Outage Scenario

A critical application's primary region (e.g., us-east-1) becomes unavailable. With Global Accelerator, traffic is instantly rerouted to the healthy secondary region (e.g., eu-west-1) via its static Anycast IPs, bypassing DNS delays and minimizing downtime.

Global Accelerator's DR Advantages

  • Static Anycast IPs: Consistent entry point, no IP changes during failover.
  • Network-Level Rerouting: Bypasses DNS caching, enabling near-instant failover.
  • Automated Health Checks: Proactive detection and redirection of traffic.
  • Reduced Downtime: Significantly lowers Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
Key Takeaway

Global Accelerator provides a superior disaster recovery solution by offering static IPs and network-level failover, ensuring faster and more reliable recovery than traditional DNS methods.

screens.title: Architectural Considerations for Global Applications
screens.narratorSegment: When designing your global application architecture with Global Accelerator, several key considerations will guide your choices to ensure optimal performance, availability, and cost-effectiveness. First, always consider the application protocol. For HTTP and HTTPS traffic, Application Load Balancers are generally the best choice, offering Layer 7 features and advanced routing. However, for high-performance TCP, UDP, or TLS passthrough, Network Load Balancers are superior due to their Layer 4 operation and ultra-low latency. Second, evaluate your performance requirements. Latency-sensitive applications like gaming or real-time trading will benefit immensely from NLBs, while standard web applications might find ALBs sufficient. Third, determine your desired level of availability and redundancy. Do you need an active/passive setup for disaster recovery, or an active/active architecture for continuous load distribution and maximum uptime? Each has its trade-offs in complexity and cost. Finally, remember that Global Accelerator's power comes from combining its global routing and health checks with the specialized capabilities of other AWS services. Always ensure your health checks are accurately configured to reflect the true health of your application, not just the underlying infrastructure. A common misconception is that Global Accelerator replaces load balancers; instead, it works in conjunction with them, enhancing their global reach. By carefully considering these factors, you can build a robust, low-latency, and highly available application that serves users worldwide.

Architectural Considerations for Global Applications

Making informed choices for your global deployment

Application Protocol

  • HTTP/S: Prefer Application Load Balancers (ALB).
  • TCP/UDP/TLS: Prefer Network Load Balancers (NLB).
  • Match endpoint to traffic type for efficiency.

Thoughtful consideration of protocol, performance, and availability is crucial for designing a resilient and efficient global application architecture with Global Accelerator.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to this masterclass on integrating AWS Global Accelerator with other essential AWS services. In today's global landscape, delivering applications with low latency and high availability across different geographic regions is paramount. Global Accelerator acts as a powerful front door, providing static Anycast IP addresses that direct user traffic over the highly optimized AWS global network. This chapter will reveal how combining Global Accelerator with services like Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, and EC2 instances creates robust, high-performance solutions. You'll learn the critical role of health checks and traffic dials in managing application availability and performance, enabling sophisticated active/passive and active/active architectures. By the end of this session, you'll understand how to design and implement a truly global, resilient application delivery strategy that significantly enhances disaster recovery capabilities. Let's explore how these integrations unlock the full potential of your cloud infrastructure.

In this chapter, we'll focus on two key learning objectives that will empower you to build advanced networking solutions. First, you will learn how to configure various AWS resources, such as Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, and even individual EC2 instances, as robust endpoints for Global Accelerator. This involves understanding the specific requirements and benefits of each endpoint type, enabling you to choose the right fit for your application's needs. For example, you'll see how an ALB provides advanced HTTP routing, while an NLB offers extreme performance for TCP/UDP traffic. Second, you'll master the implementation of health checks and traffic dials. These are crucial tools for actively managing your application's availability and performance across different AWS regions. You'll understand how Global Accelerator continuously monitors endpoint health and automatically reroutes traffic, and how traffic dials allow you to precisely control the flow of users, whether for controlled rollouts or disaster recovery scenarios. These skills are fundamental for any architect aiming to deliver highly available and performant global applications.

Continuing our journey, the next set of objectives will equip you with advanced architectural design skills. You will learn to design sophisticated multi-region active/passive and active/active architectures using Global Accelerator. This involves understanding how to configure your primary and secondary regions for seamless failover or how to distribute load efficiently across multiple active regions, ensuring both high availability and optimal user experience. For instance, an active/passive setup is ideal for disaster recovery, while active/active provides continuous load distribution. Furthermore, we'll delve into the specific benefits of integrating Global Accelerator with Elastic Load Balancers, both Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and Network Load Balancers (NLBs). You'll understand how this combination provides robust application delivery, leveraging the strengths of each service. Finally, you'll be able to discuss how Global Accelerator significantly enhances disaster recovery strategies for global applications, moving beyond traditional DNS-based failover to provide faster, more reliable recovery mechanisms. These objectives are key to mastering resilient global application deployment.

AWS Global Accelerator's true power lies in its seamless integration with various AWS services, acting as the intelligent traffic director for your global applications. At its core, Global Accelerator provides static Anycast IP addresses that serve as a single entry point for your users worldwide. It then routes traffic over the highly optimized AWS global network to specific endpoints you configure. The most common and recommended endpoint types include Application Load Balancers, or ALBs, which are ideal for HTTP and HTTPS traffic, offering advanced Layer 7 features. Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, are perfect for high-performance TCP and UDP applications, operating at Layer 4. You can also use individual EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses directly as endpoints, though this is generally reserved for specific, less scalable scenarios. Understanding these different endpoint types is crucial for designing an architecture that perfectly matches your application's protocol, performance, and availability requirements. For example, a web application would typically use an ALB, while a real-time gaming service might opt for an NLB. Global Accelerator Endpoint Types means global accelerator supports albs, nlbs, ec2 instances, and elastic ips as endpoints, allowing flexible integration with various application architectures.. In practical terms, connecting global accelerator to your aws resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Integrating Global Accelerator with Application Load Balancers, or ALBs, is a highly effective pattern for delivering web applications globally with enhanced performance and resilience. Global Accelerator directs HTTP and HTTPS traffic to the nearest healthy ALB, which then distributes these requests to your target EC2 instances or containers. This combination is powerful because the ALB provides crucial Layer 7 features, such as path-based routing, host-based routing, and SSL termination, allowing for sophisticated application-level traffic management. Meanwhile, Global Accelerator handles the global routing optimization and performs health checks at the network layer, ensuring users are always directed to the best available endpoint. For example, imagine you have an e-commerce website with ALBs deployed in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Global Accelerator will automatically route users from North America to the us-east-1 ALB and users from Europe to the eu-west-1 ALB. If the us-east-1 ALB or its targets become unhealthy, Global Accelerator seamlessly fails over traffic to the eu-west-1 ALB, providing continuous availability without relying on slow DNS changes. This setup combines the best of both worlds: Global Accelerator's global performance and static IPs with ALB's advanced request routing and application-level health checks.

For applications demanding extreme performance, ultra-low latency, and high throughput, especially those relying on non-HTTP/S protocols like TCP, UDP, or TLS passthrough, integrating Global Accelerator with Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, is the optimal choice. NLBs operate at Layer 4, the transport layer, and are engineered to handle millions of requests per second with consistent, low latency. They also provide static IP addresses for your load balancer, which can be crucial for certain network configurations. When Global Accelerator directs traffic to an NLB, it leverages the NLB's ability to forward traffic directly to target EC2 instances or containers with minimal processing overhead. This makes the combination particularly beneficial for use cases such as real-time gaming, IoT device communication, or Voice over IP, where every millisecond counts and consistent network performance is paramount. For example, a global multiplayer game could use Global Accelerator to route players to the nearest NLB, which then efficiently distributes game traffic to backend game servers. This ensures players experience the lowest possible latency, regardless of their geographic location, and provides a highly available and scalable backend for the game. The key benefit here is combining Global Accelerator's global network optimization with NLB's raw Layer 4 performance.

While Application and Network Load Balancers are the preferred endpoints for most scalable and highly available applications, Global Accelerator also offers the flexibility to use individual EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses directly as endpoints. This approach can be suitable for very specific scenarios, such as a single dedicated server that doesn't require the full features of a load balancer, or for legacy applications that are not designed to sit behind a load balancer. For example, you might have a specialized licensing server or a bastion host that needs a static global entry point without the overhead of an ALB or NLB. However, it's crucial to understand that using direct EC2 instances or Elastic IPs as endpoints comes with limitations. You lose the built-in scalability, advanced health check mechanisms, and fault tolerance that ALBs and NLBs inherently provide. If the single EC2 instance fails, Global Accelerator will reroute traffic, but you'd need to manually manage the replacement or have other mechanisms in place. Therefore, while this option exists, it's generally recommended to leverage the robust capabilities of ALBs or NLBs for any application requiring high availability, scalability, and comprehensive health monitoring. Always evaluate your application's specific needs before opting for direct instance endpoints.

A critical component of Global Accelerator's ability to deliver highly available applications is its robust health check mechanism. Global Accelerator continuously monitors the health and responsiveness of all configured endpoints. This proactive monitoring is essential for ensuring that user traffic is always directed to a healthy and operational application instance. For endpoints like Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers, Global Accelerator intelligently leverages their existing health check mechanisms. This means if an ALB determines that its backend EC2 instances are unhealthy, Global Accelerator will recognize this status. For direct EC2 instances, you configure specific health checks within Global Accelerator itself, defining the protocol, port, and path to monitor. The real power of these health checks comes into play during a failure. If an endpoint becomes unhealthy, Global Accelerator automatically and almost instantaneously stops routing traffic to it. Instead, it redirects traffic to another healthy endpoint, either within the same endpoint group or to a different endpoint group in another AWS Region. This automatic failover is significantly faster and more reliable than traditional DNS-based failover, which can suffer from DNS propagation delays due to TTLs. For example, if a database issue causes your application in us-east-1 to become unresponsive, Global Accelerator detects this and reroutes users to your healthy application in eu-west-1 within seconds, minimizing downtime and impact on your users.

Beyond automatic health-based failover, Global Accelerator provides another powerful feature for traffic management: traffic dials. A traffic dial is associated with each endpoint group, which typically corresponds to an AWS Region. This dial allows you to specify the percentage of traffic that Global Accelerator sends to that particular region. By default, a traffic dial is set to 100%, meaning the region is fully active and eligible to receive traffic. However, you can adjust this percentage to achieve various traffic management strategies. For instance, setting a region's traffic dial to 0% effectively takes it out of service, preventing any new traffic from being routed there, even if its endpoints are healthy. This is incredibly useful for maintenance, testing, or disaster recovery scenarios where you want to explicitly control traffic flow. You can also use traffic dials for controlled rollouts, gradually increasing the percentage of traffic to a new region or a new version of your application. Imagine you're deploying a new feature in ap-southeast-2. You could start by setting its traffic dial to 10%, monitoring performance, and then slowly increasing it to 50% or 100% as confidence grows. This granular control allows for sophisticated and safe deployment practices, minimizing risk during changes.

One of the most common and effective architectural patterns enabled by Global Accelerator and traffic dials is the active/passive failover strategy. In this setup, you designate one AWS Region as your primary, or active, region, which handles all normal operational traffic. A secondary, or passive, region is configured as a standby, ready to take over if the primary region experiences a complete outage or becomes unhealthy. To implement this, you would set the traffic dial for your primary region's endpoint group to 100%, ensuring all traffic flows there under normal circumstances. For your secondary, passive region, you set its traffic dial to 0%. This means Global Accelerator will not route any traffic to the secondary region unless a failover event occurs. The magic happens when Global Accelerator's health checks detect that all endpoints in the primary region have become unhealthy. In such a scenario, Global Accelerator automatically and instantly shifts all traffic to the healthy secondary region, even though its traffic dial was set to 0%. This provides a much faster and more reliable disaster recovery mechanism than traditional DNS-based failover, which can be hampered by DNS propagation delays. For example, if your primary application in us-east-1 goes offline, Global Accelerator ensures users are quickly redirected to your standby application in eu-west-1, minimizing business disruption.

In contrast to active/passive, an active/active distribution architecture leverages Global Accelerator to simultaneously serve traffic from multiple AWS Regions. This pattern is designed for maximum availability, geographic redundancy, and efficient load distribution across your global infrastructure. To implement this, you configure endpoint groups in two or more regions, and set their traffic dials to percentages that reflect their desired load distribution or capacity. For instance, you might set traffic dials to 50% for two regions, or proportionally based on the expected user base or available resources in each region. Global Accelerator then intelligently routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint across all active regions. This means a user in Europe would be routed to the European region, while a user in Asia would be routed to the Asian region, assuming both are healthy and have traffic dials set appropriately. The key benefit here is that all regions are actively serving traffic, providing continuous service even if one region experiences a partial or complete outage. If one region becomes unhealthy, Global Accelerator automatically directs all traffic to the remaining healthy regions. This not only enhances fault tolerance but also improves user experience by routing them to the closest available endpoint, reducing latency. For example, a global SaaS platform could run active instances in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-2, with Global Accelerator distributing traffic among them based on user proximity and health, ensuring optimal performance and high availability worldwide.

Disaster recovery, or DR, is a critical concern for any global application, and Global Accelerator significantly enhances DR strategies by providing a faster and more reliable failover mechanism compared to traditional DNS-based approaches. The primary challenge with DNS-based failover is propagation delay. When you update DNS records to point to a new region during a disaster, the changes can take minutes or even hours to propagate across the internet due to Time-To-Live, or TTL, settings and caching by DNS resolvers. This delay directly translates to downtime for your users. Global Accelerator, however, operates at the network layer, not the DNS layer. It provides static Anycast IP addresses that remain constant, regardless of which AWS Region is actively serving traffic. When a primary region fails, Global Accelerator's health checks detect the issue and instantly reroute traffic to a healthy endpoint in a secondary region. This rerouting happens within seconds, bypassing DNS propagation delays entirely. For example, if your primary data center in us-east-1 becomes unavailable, Global Accelerator ensures that your users' traffic is almost immediately directed to your standby application in eu-west-1, minimizing the impact of the disaster. This capability drastically reduces your Recovery Time Objective, or RTO, making Global Accelerator an invaluable tool for building resilient, business-critical applications.

When designing your global application architecture with Global Accelerator, several key considerations will guide your choices to ensure optimal performance, availability, and cost-effectiveness. First, always consider the application protocol. For HTTP and HTTPS traffic, Application Load Balancers are generally the best choice, offering Layer 7 features and advanced routing. However, for high-performance TCP, UDP, or TLS passthrough, Network Load Balancers are superior due to their Layer 4 operation and ultra-low latency. Second, evaluate your performance requirements. Latency-sensitive applications like gaming or real-time trading will benefit immensely from NLBs, while standard web applications might find ALBs sufficient. Third, determine your desired level of availability and redundancy. Do you need an active/passive setup for disaster recovery, or an active/active architecture for continuous load distribution and maximum uptime? Each has its trade-offs in complexity and cost. Finally, remember that Global Accelerator's power comes from combining its global routing and health checks with the specialized capabilities of other AWS services. Always ensure your health checks are accurately configured to reflect the true health of your application, not just the underlying infrastructure. A common misconception is that Global Accelerator replaces load balancers; instead, it works in conjunction with them, enhancing their global reach. By carefully considering these factors, you can build a robust, low-latency, and highly available application that serves users worldwide.
